abstract: The insect wing is a complex morpho-functional organ, and it remains unclear whether a set of well-defined metrics can fully capture wing-planform variation. To address this question, we digitised 339 male forewings of the European grapevine moth, Lobesia botrana (Lepidoptera: Tortricidae), an economically important grapevine pest. Specimens came from two non-overlapping seasonal flight generations. We applied two complementary shape-analysis methods - Generalised Procrustes Analysis (GPA) and Elliptic Fourier Analysis (EFA) - and correlated their principal components with four flight-related morphological metrics: aspect ratio (AR), a proxy for the second moment of wing area (MA), sweep angle (SA), and apex taper (Taper). For both methods, each of the first four principal components was most strongly correlated with its corresponding metric; together, these components represented 92.3% (GPA) and 95.7% (EFA) of the total variation of the shape. Both methods yielded concordant results, indicating that a small set of interpretable metrics captures the major axes of wing-planform variation. Generations differed significantly in mean MA, AR, and SA, and in Taper variance, consistent with seasonal phenotypic plasticity. These characters can be calculated from a small number of landmarks and therefore can serve as wing-shape markers. The analysis pipeline is implemented in the open-source MorphoGet software. This protocol provides an interpretable summary of wing-planform variation, applicable to flight-related morphology, ecology and evolution, pest monitoring, and other fields.
